beats.narration: [somber] One multiplication put a mother in prison for life.

[serious] Sally Clark, a solicitor, lost both of her infant sons in cot deaths, thirteen months apart. At her trial a paediatrician told the jury the odds of that happening naturally were one in seventy-three million. He got that number by squaring.

[thoughtful] Two probabilities multiply cleanly only when one event has no effect on the other. A family that has already lost a baby to sudden infant death is not a random family, and the Royal Statistical Society said so in writing. The correct joint uses a conditional. When the chance of a second death, given the first, is bigger than the base rate, the true joint is bigger too, and the seventy-three million evaporates.
[somber] Her conviction was overturned in two thousand three. She died four years later. The Royal Statistical Society still cites her trial when it warns courts about the misuse of statistics.
